vignette:
He was in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, hired by a geographic magazine to document the last traditional salt caravans. The terrain was brutal-slick mud under a canopy of dripping leaves, the air thick with the smell of wet earth and woodsmoke. He had been walking for three days with a local guide when they were stopped by a group of armed men. The guide tried to explain, but the men's faces were hard, their eyes moving over him like they were inspecting goods. He remembers the click of the safety on an old M16, the cold pressure of a gun barrel against his temple, and then the cloth bag thrown over his head.

For eleven weeks he was held in a bamboo hut, his wrists bound with rough nylon rope that left deep red grooves in his skin. The men spoke a language he did not understand, but he learned to read their moods by the tone of their shouts and the way they slammed the door. He was fed once a day-mushy sweet potato and sometimes a piece of gristly meat. Most of the time he was alone, staring at the mud wall, listening to the rain drumming on the roof. He tried to remember his wife's face, but after a while even her features blurred. He counted the days by the light through a crack in the wall. He lost count.

Now, three years later, he is back home in the coastal town where he and his wife moved decades ago. He is fifty-three years old. He tries to work, but photography has become a different kind of captivity. When he lifts his camera, his hands shake. The viewfinder once gave him a frame of control over the chaos of the world; now it feels like a tiny cell. He takes pictures only of empty landscapes-seascapes, empty streets, buildings with no people. If a person walks into the frame, he waits until they leave. He cannot photograph faces anymore. The eyes remind him of the men who kept him.

His wife has learned to be quiet in the morning. He wakes with a start, heart hammering, convinced he is back in the hut. The ceiling fan sounds like the rotor of an approaching helicopter. The smell of frying fish in the kitchen becomes the smell of cooking sweet potato on a smoky fire. He has to go outside to breathe. He sits on the back step and checks the perimeter of the garden three times before he can calm down.

The PCL-5 score of 62 is a number on paper. In his life, it means he cannot go to the grocery store on Saturdays because the crowded aisles make him feel trapped. It means he has stopped answering his phone because unexpected calls trigger a cold sweat. It means he replays the captivity every night in dreams that leave him gasping, and then he replays it again during the day in fragments-the taste of the cloth bag, the ache in his shoulders, the moment he heard a gunshot and thought it was his last.

His wife asked him last week to take her portrait for a family gift. He picked up the camera, adjusted the lens, and saw her face. He saw the worry lines, the gray in her hair, the love she still holds for him. He lowered the camera. "Not today," he said. He has not touched it since.
